overview: Centene is the largest managed care organization in the United States by Medicaid enrollment, administering government-sponsored and commercial health insurance for underserved and low-income populations across Medicaid, Medicare (including Wellcare-branded Medicare Advantage and standalone Part D), and ACA Marketplace (Ambetter) programs. The company operates as a multi-line health plan holding company contracting with states and CMS, covering roughly 25.7 million at-risk members as of Q3 2026 (down from 28.0 million a year earlier) across Medicaid (11.9M), Marketplace (3.4M), Medicare Advantage (~1.0M), and ~9.0M stand-alone Part D members. Headquartered in St. Louis, it also runs smaller specialty businesses (pharmacy, behavioral health via Magellan Health which is being divested, dental/vision) reported in an Other segment.

business_model.summary: Centene earns premium revenue by taking on medical risk for government-sponsored health plan members: states and CMS pay Centene a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) capitation rate, and Centene is responsible for member medical costs, with profit equal to premium less medical costs (the health benefits ratio, HBR) less administrative (SG&A) costs. The business is almost entirely recurring premium revenue under multi-year government contracts, supplemented by smaller fee-for-service/service revenue from specialty units (pharmacy, behavioral health, TPA services).

revenue_streams.name: Medicaid
revenue_streams.trend: declining (redeterminations largely complete; membership down y/y)

revenue_streams.name: Commercial (ACA Marketplace/Ambetter)
revenue_streams.trend: sharply declining (ACA enhanced-subsidy expiration cut Marketplace membership from 5.8M to 3.4M y/y)

revenue_streams.name: Medicare (Wellcare MA + stand-alone Part D/PDP)
revenue_streams.trend: mixed - MA membership declining, PDP membership growing

revenue_streams.name: Other (specialty pharmacy, behavioral health/Magellan being divested, dental/vision, TPA)

business_model.customer_type: B2G (state Medicaid agencies, CMS) with B2C distribution for Marketplace and Medicare Advantage via brokers and direct marketing
business_model.geographic_mix: US-only; Medicaid in 30 states (Florida and New York each ~10%+ of Medicaid premium revenue), Medicare Advantage in 32 states, Marketplace in 29 states, PDP in all 50 states + D.C. Revenue is concentrated in a relatively small number of large states, a structural risk.

competitive_position.market_position: Largest Medicaid managed care insurer in the US by membership (historically ~20-22% national Medicaid MCO share, well ahead of Elevance, UnitedHealthcare, Molina and CVS/Aetna); a top-5 ACA Marketplace insurer (Ambetter); a sub-scale, still-unprofitable/breakeven player in Medicare Advantage relative to UnitedHealthcare and Humana.

moat_factors.description: Largest pure-play Medicaid book gives density advantages in state contracting, actuarial data, and provider network leverage focused specifically on underserved populations that larger diversified payers deprioritize.

Multi-year state Medicaid contracts and CMS Part D/MA contracts create switching costs and procurement barriers to entry; recent Florida re-procurement retained Centene's share while removing UnitedHealth, CVS and Molina from parts of the state.
Presence across Medicaid, Medicare, and Marketplace cushions any single program's cyclicality, though all three are government-policy-dependent.
State-specific health plan brands and local provider relationships; the Wellcare brand has specific recognition in Medicare.

weaknesses: Thin, policy-set margins (HBR in the low-90s%) leave little buffer against medical cost trend surprises
Heavy dependence on volatile, abruptly-changing government policy (ACA subsidies, Medicaid rates, CMS Star ratings/MA benchmarks) rather than product differentiation
Medicare Advantage remains sub-scale and not yet consistently profitable versus UnitedHealthcare/Humana
2025 forecasting failure (Marketplace risk-adjustment miscall, guidance withdrawal, $6.7B goodwill impairment) damaged credibility with investors and complicates near-term guidance trust
State revenue concentration (FL, NY) creates outsized exposure to any single state's budget or re-procurement decision

growth_drivers: Medicare Advantage and stand-alone Part D (PDP) expansion under the Wellcare brand, targeting profitability improvement/breakeven after years of investment
Corrective 2026 Marketplace repricing (implemented in states covering ~95% of membership) aimed at restoring Ambetter margins even as membership shrinks
Medicaid re-procurement wins and rate adequacy advocacy as states true-up capitation rates to reflect post-redetermination acuity

Specialty/ancillary business optimization and portfolio simplification via divestitures (Magellan Health sale, prior disposals of Circle Health, Collaborative Health Systems, Magellan Specialty Health)
Capital return: expanded $2.0B buyback authorization (Oct 2026) and continued debt paydown ($1.1B reduced since mid-2026) as the balance sheet delevers
New leadership structure (Group Presidents for Markets/Commercial and Medicare/Specialty, reporting to CEO Sarah London) intended to sharpen segment execution and accountability

business.description: Consolidated HBR rose from 88.3% (FY2024) to 91.9% (FY2025) and ran 92.7% in Q3 2026 (flat y/y but still elevated); driven by accelerated medical cost trend, higher Medicaid acuity post-redetermination, new high-cost specialty drugs, and Marketplace morbidity mis-pricing. Government-capped pricing gives Centene limited ability to pass through cost surprises in-year.

Expiration of enhanced ACA premium tax credits (APTCs), the ACA 'Final Rule,' and OBBBA provisions drove Marketplace membership down from 5.83M to 3.40M y/y (Q3 2026); management has guided to further 2026 membership declines, shrinking a segment that was ~21% of revenue.

July 2025 guidance withdrawal followed a ~$1.8B miss in expected Marketplace risk-adjustment transfers identified by outside actuary Wakely; the single-day ~40% stock decline highlighted weaknesses in the company's own cost/morbidity forecasting.
Florida and New York each represent 10%+ of Medicaid premium revenue; loss or unfavorable repricing in a top state would be financially material.
MA membership (~954K) is small relative to UnitedHealthcare/Humana, and the segment has struggled to reach consistent profitability amid CMS Star rating and risk-adjustment pressure.

Company offered voluntary buyouts to its ~61,000-person workforce in 2026 (reportedly ~$276M in severance costs) as it rightsizes for a smaller Marketplace book; execution risk on cost takeout without harming service quality.

financial.description: Consolidated indebtedness of roughly $15.5-17.4B; variable-rate exposure and debt-to-capital covenants under its credit facility; FY2025 operating cash flow swung from $154M (2024) to $5.1B (2025) partly reflecting working-capital/claims-timing volatility, while Q3 2026 operating cash flow was negative (~$(3.7)B), underscoring cash flow lumpiness.

FY2025 included a $6.7B non-cash goodwill impairment (triggered by OBBBA-related market deterioration and a falling stock price), plus a $513M Magellan Health impairment and $55M intangible write-off, producing a $6.67B GAAP net loss for 2025 despite $1.0B of adjusted net earnings.
State insurance regulators can delay or deny dividends from regulated health plan subsidiaries up to the parent, constraining capital flexibility in stress scenarios.

regulatory.description: Expiration of enhanced APTCs enacted during COVID-era legislation, combined with the 2025 ACA Program Integrity 'Final Rule' and OBBBA provisions, is reshaping Marketplace eligibility, verification, and risk pools; any further federal action (or a renewal of subsidies) would materially swing Marketplace economics either direction.

regulatory.risk: Medicaid redetermination and state budget pressure
regulatory.description: Post-pandemic Medicaid eligibility redeterminations have largely run through the base, leaving a smaller, higher-acuity membership; future state rate-setting may lag actual acuity/cost trend, and OBBBA-driven federal Medicaid funding/work-requirement changes add further uncertainty to state budgets and eligibility rules.

CMS's draft 2027 Medicare Advantage rate notice was viewed by management as insufficient to cover medical trend; PDP bids for 2026 came in below CMS benchmarks in all 34 regions, pressuring stand-alone Part D economics; Inflation Reduction Act redesign of Part D increases Centene's drug cost risk exposure.

Ongoing exposure to state/federal program audits, False Claims Act and fraud-and-abuse litigation, data privacy requirements, and risk-adjustment/encounter-data accuracy disputes that can trigger repayments or penalties.

macro.description: As an almost entirely government-payor-funded business, Centene's revenue is directly exposed to federal and state fiscal policy, appropriations, and political shifts (e.g., Medicaid expansion rollbacks, subsidy expiration) rather than conventional macroeconomic cycles.
Elevated medical cost trend (higher utilization, specialty drug pricing, behavioral health demand) outpacing capitation rate increases is squeezing margins across the industry, not just Centene.
Variable-rate debt and investment portfolio yields give some interest-rate sensitivity, but the business is not capital-intensive or rate-cycle-driven in the way consumer-discretionary names are.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US managed care is navigating a post-pandemic unwind: Medicaid redeterminations have shrunk and re-acuitized state rolls, enhanced ACA subsidies have lapsed causing a steep (CBO estimated ~25%, actual industry commentary suggests 35%+) Marketplace enrollment decline, and Medicare Advantage/Part D face tightening CMS rates and IRA-driven drug cost redesign. Across the industry (Centene, UnitedHealth, Elevance, Humana, Molina), 2025 was marked by a broad medical-cost-trend reset and depressed margins; 2026 guidance from most payers (including Centene) reflects repricing actions intended to restore margin.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low traditional macro cyclicality (demand for healthcare is non-discretionary) but high policy cyclicality tied to election outcomes, state budgets, and federal legislation (ACA, Medicaid expansion, OBBBA).
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-to-moderate: modest variable-rate debt exposure and investment portfolio income sensitivity.
key_input_costs: Behavioral health and home health utilization

recent_developments.event: Centene withdrew FY2025 guidance after an outside actuarial review (Wakely) found Marketplace risk-adjustment transfer revenue would be about $1.8B lower than expected and morbidity assumptions were too optimistic; stock fell a record ~40% in a single day.

Q3 2025 10-K/10-Q period: recorded a $6,723M non-cash goodwill impairment plus a $513M Magellan Health impairment, triggered by OBBBA-related market deterioration and the depressed stock price; consolidated HBR hit 91.9% for the full year.

Agreed to divest the remaining Magellan Health behavioral-health businesses, continuing the company's portfolio simplification after earlier sales of Magellan Rx, Magellan Specialty Health, Circle Health and Collaborative Health Systems.
Filed FY2025 10-K confirming a $6.67B GAAP net loss for 2025 versus $3.3B net income in 2024, while adjusted net earnings were $1.0B.

Announced a new executive leadership structure, creating Group President roles for Markets & Commercial (Daniel Finke) and Medicare & Specialty (Michael Carson), both reporting to CEO Sarah London, to sharpen segment accountability.

Began offering voluntary employee buyouts across its ~61,000-person workforce as it rightsizes the organization for a smaller post-subsidy-expiration Marketplace book, incurring meaningful severance costs.

Reported Q3 2026 results: revenue $50.6B (up from $49.7B y/y), HBR 92.7% (flat y/y, better than expected on Medicare), adjusted diluted EPS $0.58, GAAP diluted loss per share $(0.14). Marketplace membership fell to 3.40M from 5.83M a year earlier as enhanced ACA subsidies lapsed; total at-risk membership fell to 25.7M from 28.0M. Raised FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance to >$5.20 (+$0.40) and narrowed full-year HBR guidance to 90.4%-91.1%. Redeemed remaining 2027 senior notes and expanded the buyback program by $2.0B.

items.notes: Raised by $0.40 from prior guidance after a better-than-expected Q3, driven mainly by Medicare segment outperformance.
Gap to adjusted EPS reflects non-recurring/special items excluded from the adjusted figure (restructuring, divestiture-related items).
Midpoint ~90.75%, a 15 bps improvement versus prior guidance range; Q3 2026 actual HBR was 92.7%, flat with Q3 2025 but ahead of internal expectations.
Reflects continued Marketplace membership attrition offset by Medicare/PDP growth and Medicaid rate increases.
Core underwriting revenue base, excluding other service-type revenue.
Reflects cost discipline initiatives including 2026 workforce buyouts to rightsize for a smaller Marketplace membership base.
Benefiting from debt paydown, including full redemption of 2027 senior notes in October 2026.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Sarah London cited 'solid core fundamentals' and said earnings are recovering faster than previously expected, with Q3 HBR outperformance led by Medicare while Medicaid and Marketplace tracked to plan. Management reiterated that the combined effect of expired enhanced APTCs, the ACA Program Integrity Final Rule, and OBBBA provisions will keep pressuring 2026 Marketplace membership, and that 2026 Marketplace rates were refiled in states covering ~95% of membership to reflect a higher morbidity baseline. Management also flagged that CMS's draft 2027 Medicare Advantage rate notice (released Jan 2026) was, in its view, insufficient to cover medical cost trend, and that 2026 PDP bids came in below CMS benchmarks in all 34 regions.

bull_case: Largest scale player in Medicaid managed care, with incumbency advantages in state contracting (e.g., Florida re-procurement retained share) that are difficult for new entrants to replicate

FY2026 guidance raises (adjusted EPS >$5.20, HBR narrowed to 90.4-91.1%) signal that the worst of the 2025 cost/actuarial miss may be behind the company, with Medicare segment outperformance providing an early proof point
Aggressive 2026 Marketplace repricing, workforce rightsizing, and portfolio simplification (Magellan divestiture) should improve margin quality even on a smaller revenue base
Balance sheet deleveraging (debt down to ~$15.5B, 2027 notes fully redeemed) and an expanded $2.0B buyback authorization provide a capital-return tailwind as cash generation normalizes
Depressed valuation and analyst price targets (consensus roughly $65-75, some bull cases to $80+) following the 2025 crash leave room for re-rating if margin recovery proves durable through 2027
bear_case: Marketplace membership has already collapsed from 5.8M to 3.4M (Q3 2026) following ACA enhanced-subsidy expiration, structurally shrinking a business line that was over a fifth of revenue, with further declines guided

HBR remains elevated (92.7% in Q3 2026, versus 87.7% in FY2022/23) and the FY2026 guided range of 90.4-91.1% is still well above pre-2024 levels, raising the question of whether a ~88% HBR era is permanently behind the company

2025's forecasting failure (actuarial miss, guidance withdrawal, 40% single-day stock drop, $6.7B goodwill write-off) damaged management credibility and makes near-term guidance harder for investors to trust at face value

Business is almost entirely a bet on US government healthcare policy (Medicaid funding/work requirements under OBBBA, ACA subsidy renewal politics, CMS Medicare Advantage/Part D rate-setting), all of which are outside management's control and subject to abrupt legislative or regulatory change
Medicare Advantage remains sub-scale and not yet durably profitable relative to UnitedHealthcare and Humana, limiting the segment's ability to offset continued Medicaid/Marketplace margin pressure
